#5607. Thanksgiving Costs at Home Jump 6% in 2026 as Grocery and Utility Bills Hit Hosts Hard

Thanksgiving is the perfect time for loved ones to gather over a delicious, hearty meal. But in 2026, that feast could come with a higher price tag than we’d like.

According to the American Farm Bureau, the average cost of a 10-person holiday dinner will rise by 6% from 2025 to $5.86 per person. That’s because staples like turkey, milk, rolls, and cranberries have shot up in price.

And unfortunately, the higher price tag doesn’t stop at the grocery store. You may also notice a spike in your utility bills as your home’s systems are forced to work harder to keep everyone comfortable.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) found that the average family already uses over 300 gallons of water per day at home. With increased usage from additional showers, dishwashing, and hand-washing that are typical during the holidays, costs are sure to climb.

“Having guests over greatly drives up money spent on groceries, but it also drives up utility costs. Preparing all of that food often involves keeping ovens and burners running for multiple hours and using large amounts of water in both the cooking and cleaning processes,” explains Carrie Barnard, founder and recipe developer at Eating on a Dime.

Fortunately, it’s still possible to enjoy Thanksgiving without breaking the bank. A bit of planning and creativity can help keep your grocery expenses and utility bill in check.

Where you live can also impact how much you spend this Thanksgiving.

The American Farm Bureau found that the 10-person classic dinner in the Northeast is about 5% higher than the national average of $61.57.

Costs in the West ($58.74) and Midwest ($56.89) are closer to the national average. And if you live in the South, you could expect to pay around $54.33.

There are a few reasons for these cost differences.

“They largely have to do with supply chains, since different regions require different imports, and these imprints cost more the further they travel,” says Barnard.

Since the Northeast is generally colder, it relies more heavily on imports for many Thanksgiving staples, which leads to a higher cost for consumers. Also, the Northeast typically has higher operating costs for businesses, meaning that grocery prices are often higher.

“However, prices vary widely between different stores, and many of them offer special holiday promotions, so there are usually savings to be found,” Barnard adds.

While grocery and energy costs may be higher this Thanksgiving, these tips can help reduce them and enjoy the holiday without overspending.

Jim Wang, founder at Wallet Hacks in Fulton, MD, suggests exploring promotions at your local supermarkets and groceries.

“Many stores know consumers are being squeezed and often try to put out promos around Thanksgiving. They may offer the turkey at a low cost to get you to make your entire holiday purchase there,” Wang explains.

Depending on how you celebrate Thanksgiving and who attends your meal, a potluck might make sense.

“Every year, we do a potluck with friends and everyone brings something to share. This defrays the costs across everyone and while you don't end up with nearly as many leftovers, that's also excess spending you can avoid, especially if Thanksgiving leftovers don't excite you,” says Wang.

If you’re hosting, be a bit more conservative about how much everyone will eat.

“Sometimes we get concerned about having guests leave hungry and we make too much as a result,” Wang says.

It’s perfectly OK to make less of the more expensive items, like proteins, and bigger portions of sides that they can fill up on. Chances are your guests may prefer those sides to the turkey anyway.

Barnard tries to use her air fryer and slow cooker rather than my full oven when possible.

“These appliances are highly versatile and able to cook a wide variety of dishes, and they consume much less energy in the process,” explains Barnard.

Unlike ovens, which leak out heat and consume more energy the more you open the door to check on your food, air fryers and slow cookers cook things quickly and efficiently with low energy.

“I try to only use the oven when it’s required due to the size or amount of food involved,” Barnard adds.

#5606. Leading With Purpose

https://www.ironvalleyrealestate.com/region/hamptonroads

Region served: Coastal Virginia and Northern North Carolina

Work philosophy that you live by: Together, we’ll go further.

What drew you to Iron Valley Real Estate that made you want to step into ownership, and how does the brand’s structure and vision help your team stand out in the market?

What resonated most was the model, which was very agent friendly, where agents kept the majority of their money. But the company leaders are what ultimately attracted me to ownership. Mike Little and Eric Edwards, the original founders, allowed me to have a platform where I was able to train and mentor a big group of agents, giving me free reign. I got to incorporate my own philosophies into what was already a successful brokerage, and I came with a diverse group of agents who added to the culture of Iron Valley. The fact that the ownership embraced that diversity is what ultimately led to me wanting to be a part of it.

How has your 23-year experience in the Navy translated to your real estate career, especially when it comes to mentoring agents?

A large part of my success has been the leadership training that I received in the Navy—the years of guiding and leading a diverse group of individuals. The military is very diverse, where people come from different races, religions, ethnicities, parts of the world and even parts of the United States. Bringing all these different people together, the military teaches you how to interact with others at a large scale. On top of the diversity, the leadership training I had throughout my time in the Navy helped catapult my real estate career.

What is your best piece of advice for those considering brokerage ownership or leadership roles?

Understand that your job satisfaction isn’t going to come from finances or money. This has to be a person whose job satisfaction comes from helping other people excel. A lot of people get into the brokerage and real estate ownership business thinking that it’s profitable—and while it can be, if that’s your sole reason for opening a brokerage, you’re never going to attain that job satisfaction. I want to excel with the people I enjoy being around; I don’t want to make it to the top alone.

When onboarding new agents or taking experienced agents to the next level, how do you foster accountability while maintaining a supportive environment?

I remind them of their “why.” In order to hold someone accountable to reach the goals they’ve set for themselves, you have to remind them why they want to achieve those goals in the first place. For me, my why is seeing everyone I encounter achieve whatever success means to them.

How do you train your team to handle the fast-paced timelines, permanent change of station moves and VA loan nuances that come with serving military families in your community?

Hampton Roads is the biggest military concentrated area in the United States. Every agent knows someone who served, has a family member who served, or served themselves. And if that’s not the case, which doesn’t happen very often, I actually teach military jargon. We also go over the processes associated with military members moving and selecting orders—and if they have to leave the area, we examine what that process looks like as well. Our owners are all veterans, so we train to those experiences to ensure our agents are better equipped to serve the military population.

For more information, please visit https://www.ironvalleyrealestate.com.

Paige Brown is the managing editor, blog/social media for RISMedia.

#5605. Chris Simms Scores a $4.5 Million NYC Home—Weeks After Selling His Longtime Connecticut Retreat

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Chris Simms has picked up a $4.5 million New York City residence—after offloading his longtime Connecticut estate for $5.5 million.

The 45-year-old—who retired from the NFL in 2010 following a spleen injury—and his wife, Daniella, recently picked up the property, which is located in Sutton Tower.

His new pad comes complete with three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, and floor-to-ceiling windows, according to the New York Post, who first reported the sale. The property also boasts a chef's kitchen and panoramic views.

The Sutton Place tower was built in 2022 by architect Thomas Juul-Hansen. The residence is known to be the tallest tower on the East Side.

As a member of the luxe dwelling, Simms and his wife get access to a resort-style pool, a gym, a personal training studio, saunas, and a spa space.

His purchase came weeks after Realtor.com® exclusively revealed that he sold his Connecticut property for $5.5 million.

He initially put their longtime Greenwich abode on the market on Feb. 6. Within a matter of months, they had dropped the price by $500,000.

A second price cut in June slashed a further $600,000 from the ask, while a third discount on Aug. 21 saw the athlete's original ask of $8 million lowered to $6.2 million, a move that ultimately bagged a buyer for Simms' dwelling.

Simms, who now serves as an analyst for NBC Sports, purchased the home for $2.5 million in 2019—shortly after he and his wife invested heavily in its restoration and renovation.

The property, which was originally built in 1725, has been updated extensively in the seven years since the couple took ownership.

Today, the property is hailed as a "piece of Greenwich history" with all the luxury of a modern mansion.

"A fully restored antique farmhouse offering approximately 3,669 square feet of refined living space, set on extraordinary level acreage with sweeping meadow views and an irreplaceable country setting across from protected conservation land with direct access to the Greenwich Riding Trails," the listing, which was held by Monica Webster of Douglas Elliman, noted.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom dwelling features an open floor plan that begins with a living area with a cozy fireplace, windows, and wooden beams on the ceiling.

The chef's kitchen boasts state-of-the-art appliances, a white marble island, and white cabinetry.

The charming dining area also has wooden beams on the ceiling and a wooden island.

The bedrooms follow the home's minimalistic aesthetic and feature enough space for a queen-sized bed while boasting small windows.

"The residence blends historic authenticity with modern luxury, featuring wide-plank antique floors, exposed beams, preserved fireplaces, and original architectural details," the listing added.

The bathrooms feature double vanities, a large glass-enclosed shower, a marble soaking tub, and sliding barn doors.

Elsewhere, there is a gym, spa center with a massage chair, and an outdoor entertaining area with a foosball table.

Throughout the home, modern aesthetics have been meticulously merged with historic charm.

"A thoughtful renovation delivers elevated comfort throughout, including a newly created primary suite with cathedral ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, a bespoke dressing room, and a private staircase to a serene, light-filled office and library retreat for everyday living," the listing stated.

Simms and his wife lived in Greenwich for many years, having previously sold another dwelling in the area for $2.7 million before relocating to their farmhouse.

They chose the farmhouse for its impressive parcel, noting to the outlet that they wanted more space for their horses.

However, they are now choosing to call to New York home.

Before settling down in Connecticut, Simms enjoyed a lengthy career in the NFL, a career that began at the University of Texas at Austin, after which he was drafted by the Buccaneers as the last pick of the final round in the 2003 NFL draft.

Simms remained with Tampa Bay until 2008, when he was released by the team. He was later picked up by the Tennessee Titans, with whom he played for a year before moving on to the Denver Broncos.

After a brief return to the Titans, the quarterback's career came to an end, with many pointing to a 2006 spleen injury as the reason for his retirement from the NFL.

He briefly tried his hand at coaching, signing with the New England Patriots in 2012 as an offensive coach, as well as a scouting expert, but he made a move into broadcasting after just a few months.

Simms and his wife, who met in high school, tied the knot in 2004 and now share two children.

Anthropic’s growth story helps explain the appetite. Its annualized revenue run rate reportedly reached $81 billion by October 31, while New Street Research projects revenue could exceed $500 billion by 2030.

Bitcoin has already suffered a substantial decline ahead of Anthropic’s debut. BTC fell 23% during the 50 days preceding Anthropic’s expected listing. That closely resembles the 19% decline during the 50 days before SpaceX began trading in June.

Yet, the SpaceX comparison becomes more interesting when examining what happened after its debut. SpaceX launched its record-breaking IPO at $135 per share on June 12. Shares closed their first trading session at $160.95, gaining 19.2%.

The stock subsequently climbed nearly 40% during its first week, briefly pushing its valuation above $2 trillion. Bitcoin did not collapse during the listing. It was trading around $63,500, remaining almost flat over 24 hours. Crypto markets eventually recovered alongside the wider risk-on move.

It was somewhat expected; a $64 billion public offering creates a substantial new destination for investors. So, even a small shift in portfolio allocations could matter when crypto liquidity is already under pressure.

Nvidia has given the AI investment narrative another powerful boost. The chipmaker reported third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion, beating analyst expectations of $109.11 billion. Revenue increased 103% year over year, while its fourth-quarter revenue forecast reached $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. Nvidia shares gained 4% in extended trading following the results.

The earnings beat reinforces the investment case behind Anthropic’s IPO. AI infrastructure spending continues expanding, and investors have another opportunity to buy into that growth through public equity markets.

There is an interesting twist: Nvidia itself is committing $10 billion to Anthropic’s private placement. The same company delivering the latest earnings catalyst is helping finance one of the largest anticipated stock market debuts.

This creates a difficult competitive environment for Bitcoin. Institutional investors can now choose between established AI infrastructure leaders, rapidly growing AI developers, and crypto exposure.

Anthropic’s debut is more than another technology listing. It could become a defining test of Bitcoin’s ability to compete for investor attention during the AI boom.

If Anthropic prices above $78 and its shares rally strongly after the debut, Bitcoin could come under further pressure. But if the IPO excitement fades after its debut, crypto could regain some of the attention currently flowing toward AI stocks.

#5603. Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate

Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine update to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk.

Researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space.

How the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday.

The researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

The malware itself is delivered through a .pth file added to both releases, a type of file Python runs every time it starts, meaning the credential stealer runs even if the framework itself is never imported. The two versions also kept the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0 as a dependency, so the framework continued to work normally while the malware ran in the background.

Once running, the malware collects secrets from environment variables and from other running processes, along with credential files for services such as Azure, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face. It also requests Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, according to application security company Endor Labs Inc., with the second version adding requests for GitHub Actions tokens. The stolen data is then compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site address controlled by the attacker.

Researchers at malware tracking site OpenSourceMalware described the malware as a “focused credential and token stealer, not a remote access trojan,” noting that it does not install any persistence on infected systems.

Wiz’s analysis suggests the number of victims may be small, though it covers only the 50 requests the attacker’s free webhook.site account retained. Of those, 17 represented only three unique successful thefts of victim data, with the rest coming from the attacker’s own machines and from sandbox and security vendor scanning.

The incident is not the first this year involving an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Microsoft’s durabletask package was hijacked after its PyPI token was stolen in an attack that has been linked to TeamPCP, the group also behind the compromise of LiteLLM. Wiz says it has not linked the two incidents.

Anyone who installed either of the malicious versions is being urged to treat it as a credential compromise, according to researchers, who recommend rebuilding from version 1.26.0 and rotating any secrets the affected systems could access.

“A list of dependencies in production might show no trace of the framework, while a build runner could have installed it and been shut down before the alert arrived,” James Matchett, head of security at software supply chain security company Cloudsmith Ltd., told SiliconANGLE.

“If that runner had access to a deployment token, the team needs to know which version it installed and what the token could access,” he added.

#5602. Perez Hilton Returns to Miami Residence—After Hospitalization for At-Home Health Incident

Perez Hilton has returned to his Miami residence after a health incident left him hospitalized.

The 48-year-old was hospitalized in August following a distressing livestream that prompted several calls to police and requests for a welfare check.

Officers ultimately transported Hilton to a nearby hospital, while mental health professionals and the Crisis Response Unit offered support to his friends and family.

Hilton received treatment for multiple broken bones and significant blood loss. After undergoing surgery, he was transferred to an inpatient medical facility.

Now, his family has revealed that Hilton is “back with his family while continuing his recovery through an intensive outpatient program.”

They noted that he is getting "ongoing therapy" and "mental health support."

“Over the past few weeks, Perez has enjoyed several successful weekend visits with his mom and children. Being reunited with his loved ones has meant so much to everyone, especially after these past few difficult months. With Thanksgiving approaching, we’re looking forward to spending some much-needed quality time together as a family and enjoying a little peace and quiet during the holiday," the statement continued.

In September, his family shared an update on the situation as they begged fans to vacate his property.

The message revealed that before the livestream event, Hilton's "children, niece, and sister were inside the home."

"When it became clear that Perez was experiencing a severe mental health crisis and harming himself, they immediately fled to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma," the message continued.

Hilton's family previously revealed that he was receiving medical care and was "able to communicate."

The update came after Hilton opened about his move to Realtor.com®, reflecting on what he'll miss most about his property and his fond memories of Las Vegas.

“It is a beautiful home, and it served me well personally and professionally," he said. "I filmed tons of television segments and news interviews from this home, and produced two documentaries.

"I would film every day for my socials, and livestream as well, and I do a lot of talking head commentary work. I filmed tons of specials for different networks and streamers in my home and outdoors. It's just so beautiful,"

"All three of my favorite spaces in the home have one thing in common—they are all very healing for me. The primary bath has the biggest, most luxurious shower that I've ever had, and the closet is huge and has so much space. Also, I never had my own, dedicated office before, and I really loved that. It's just the perfect home for a family. Everybody has space," he added.

Speaking about the property's location, Hilton told Realtor.com, "It was important for me to be close to the Strip, but it’s equal distance to Summerlin and everywhere we needed to be. My children’s schools, doctors, and dentists were all just a few minutes away.”

Hilton was especially pleased with the fact that his mother had her own private living space. One of home designer Blue Heron's signature features is a "NexGen Suite," and, because he bought the home before it was finished, he got to customize elements of the layout to ensure they were perfect for his mom.

“This was perfect for me, because my mother is a huge part of my family,” said Hilton. “She’s both grandmother and co-parent to my children. To be able to give her the space that she deserves was important. She had her own entrance, her own living room and kitchenette area."

However, despite his love for Nevada, Hilton noted that he is confident in his decision.

"It just feels like the right move, the only move, to make at this time. I've loved Las Vegas, but it's time to be closer to family," he added.

The property is being sold with Kathryn Winterton of Las Vegas Sotheby’s real estate agency, who told Realtor.com, "This home was designed for the way people want to live and entertain today. The natural light, open spaces, and seamless connection to the backyard create an atmosphere that feels both sophisticated and welcoming."

The home spans 7,000 square feet and boasts several modern living spaces, as well as a resort-style pool.

As in so many family dwellings, Hilton says the kitchen is the heart of the home, with its premium appliances, sleek custom cabinetry and a massive dining and prep island.

The kitchen opens up to the high-ceiling living and dining areas, which feel expansive, welcoming and luxurious. Generous walls of glass provide abundant natural light create a light, airy atmosphere.

Outdoors on the acre lot there's a pool, spa, lush landscaping and multiple outdoor gathering spaces. Hilton said he did a lot of his production work outside, as there are a variety of luxurious backdrops ideal for his commentary.

Set in a chic, private gated neighborhood known as Prado, Hilton enjoyed the fact that the home is on a corner lot in a small community with fewer than 20 homes.

Hilton and his family enjoyed the home, the community and Las Vegas in general so much he says he feels a bit of guilt moving his family away. But "kids are adaptable," he says. He knows this from experience.

A little over three years ago, Hilton packed up his three children and his mother and moved to Las Vegas from Los Angeles, the city where he had infinite Hollywood connections and a luxe, six bedroom, five bath classic Spanish Colonial built in 1926.

Prior to that, Hilton and his family lived in New York City for several years.

Hilton took to Instagram to explain the reasoning behind his move from Las Vegas, where he has been living for the past 3.5 years.

"We’re moving permanently to Miami. I am so excited, not nervous. I know this is the right move for me and my children and my mother," he said at the beginning of the video.

Although Hilton insisted he has "nothing but wonderful memories" while calling Nevada home, he claimed that his decision to relocate to the Sunshine State came from a higher power.

Hilton, who has three children via surrogacy, said a large part of his decision to move was due to his difficult year, which was filled with several health scares, including a 21-day hospital stay and a blood clot.

#5600. Lot Supply Rises for Ninth Consecutive Quarter

The supply of vacant developed lots continued to loosen in the third quarter as slower construction activity brought the national lot market further into balance, according to Zonda.

Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index rose to 88.5 in the third quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier and 3.9% from the second quarter. It marked the ninth consecutive quarterly increase in the index.

The index measures the supply of single-family vacant developed lots relative to the rate at which builders absorb those lots through housing starts. Zonda rated the national market “appropriately supplied” in the third quarter.

In the second quarter, the index sat at the boundary between “slightly undersupplied” and “appropriately supplied.” The third-quarter increase placed the national market in the latter category.

“The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” says Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market.”

Fergus noted that affordability pressures and widespread incentives continue to challenge builders’ ability to convert demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market indicates that lot availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction, he said, but does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost pressures have disappeared.

Lot supply increased year over year in every major metropolitan area tracked by Zonda except Boise, Idaho. Among the markets where supply increased, the average annual gain was 32%.

Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle posted the largest year-over-year increases in lot supply. Boise was the only market where supply tightened, with its index falling from 65.7 in the third quarter of 2025 to 51.9.

Despite the broader improvement in availability, 12 of the 30 markets tracked by Zonda remained “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed supply ratings during the quarter, Zonda points out.

Zonda also reported a modest increase in the future lot pipeline. Total upcoming lots increased 1% year over year and 1.6% from the second quarter.

Upcoming lots include properties in the later stages of development that are typically expected to become vacant developed lots within 12 to 18 months.

The increase suggests additional lots are moving toward delivery, although the pipeline is expanding much more slowly than the current supply index. The divergence reflects the role of softer starts in loosening lot conditions: available lots are lasting longer as builders respond to weaker demand and elevated mortgage rates.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5599. Resolve AI’s SRE-1 model finds root causes of production alerts as AI agents go on call

Incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

The new model, announced Wednesday, reflects the company’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan said Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

In testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

Primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in production are said to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

Salesforce Inc. is among the early users. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, said that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”

“No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” said Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”

Primary On-call is now generally available. Access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI’s own platform.

Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

#5598. The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs

Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment.

Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true.

Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.

These programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable.

First-time homebuyers, often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help.

The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan.

Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment.

While 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance, or PMI, which is assessed because lenders believe the loan carries risk. This in turn raises the homebuyer’s monthly expenses.

Here's an example: PMI is typically 0.5% to 1% of the loan amount per year. So if buyers put down less than 20% and their mortgage is $300,000, their PMI would be between $1,500 and $3,000 per year. That would add about $125 to $250 per month on top of their mortgage payment, a significant charge. (Homeowners can have PMI canceled when the equity in their home surpasses 20%.)

So, while a buyer can also choose loans that require a down payment of just a single digit, that PMI can stretch a budget paper-thin. That's where down payment assistance can help.

At least 2,000 such programs exist across the country. Some are federal, but most tend to be at state and local levels, which is important to know when searching for help. Private organizations, from lenders to nonprofits, also work with borrowers who need help.

These programs might offer grants, loans, tax credits, or a combination of a couple of these benefits. Funding can come from our government, nonprofits, and private enterprises. Let’s take a closer look:

Grants might be the most desirable form of down payment assistance. Typically, a grant is fully forgiven at closing and never has to be paid back. Yes, we’re talking about free money!

About 7% of down payment help comes in the form of grants, says Veronica Khandelwal, vice president of HFA Relations at Down Payment Resource, which provides consumers with guidance on this kind of assistance. But there is a catch.

“Grants require owner occupancy," she says of the requirement for buyers to live in these properties. That's to make sure these loans don't go to investors or vacation-home buyers. "Some programs allow grants to be applied to multifamily purchases of one to four units so long as one of the units is occupied by the borrower."

Forgivable loans are another option. These loans need to be repaid only if a repayment trigger event occurs, such as the home being sold before the end of the term, the home being no longer owner-occupied, the title being transferred, or the loan being defaulted on.

Deferred-payment loans are also available. These are paid back either at the end of the loan term or if a repayment trigger occurs. So, while it’s not a gift, it will help homebuyers get over that down payment hurdle and buy a house they might otherwise not have been able to afford.

Repayable loans are another leg up on homeownership. They require borrowers to make monthly payments, like a typical loan. But here's the good part: They do so at interest rates starting as low as 0%. That helps spread the down payment and closing costs over a number of years, making it much easier to enter the housing market.

Some agencies also offer a combination of these forms of assistance. That could mean that a portion of the help will be forgiven (or “written off” with no repayment needed), while some will need to be repaid. Tax credits are sometimes offered as well, further sweetening the deal.

Each down payment assistance program will have its own rules and guidelines, but the vast majority are offered only for a home that buyers will live in as a primary residence.

Here are some of the more popular national options folks might access to help them to pivot from home shopper to homebuyer.

FHA (Federal Housing Authority) loans were created by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for first-time homeowners (HUD). These mortgages allow as little as 3.5% for the down payment, provided buyers have a credit score of 580 or higher, along with other qualifying factors. The federal government insures these loans, and for that reason, banks are more willing to loan money to homebuyers who have neither top-tier credit nor loads of cash to put down on the purchase.

FHA Section 203(k) loans require only 3% down, provided qualifying buyers will live in the property, typically one that needs work, while they fix it up. For buyers hoping for a DIY route into a dream home, this could be a win-win. The cost of improvements is included in the loan so buyers can finance both the home and up to $35,000 in repairs.

But buyers beware: The cost of materials and construction labor has spiked since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and work is taking much longer to be completed than ever before.

VA (U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs) loans might be offered directly by the VA or backed by the department. Several factors are considered, such as service history, duty status, income, and credit rating. But those who qualify can purchase a home with zero down as long as the sales price isn’t higher than the home’s appraised value.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are federally funded loans that can help buyers skirt steep down payments. The Home Possible, HomeReady, and HomeOne loans typically offer a 3% down payment mortgage to qualifying, lower-income homebuyers.

Good Neighbor Next Door is another HUD-sponsored program. In this case, law enforcement officers, teachers, firefighters, and emergency medical technicians can enjoy a substantial incentive in the form of a discount of 50% from the list price of the home in a community that is being revitalized. The buyer must live in the house for three years as a primary residence.

Teacher Next Door Grant is a program similar to the one above but is designed to help educators own their own homes. Grants to the tune of up to $8,000 in certain areas are possible with additional down payment assistance available in some circumstances.

The USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) Rural Home Loan Program was created to assist people buying homes in rural locations. For qualifying, single-family properties, loans might be available with no money down. There are maximum income limits and other qualifications to be eligible for one of these mortgages.

There are plenty of other programs available as well. Different states and cities, as well as individual lenders and nonprofits, can help prospective homebuyers get the financing they need. Folks should put their location and "down payment assistance" into a search engine, and take a look at what's available. They might see everything from Habitat for Humanity to local religious organizations pop up. Also,visit Down Payment Resource.

One other path to explore is whether a buyer's job provides down payment assistance. A lot of employers may offer assistance in  the form of a $10,000 loan that is forgivable after five years.

Down payments hit a four-year low at the start of 2026. The median payment fell to $23,400 and 12.8% in Q1 2026, down 19% and 1.2 ppts year over year.

However, down payments remain well above pre-pandemic levels, as more buying is happening in the lower-down-payment South and Midwest, even as the Northeast stays deeply competitive.

The Northeast posted the highest median down payment at $57,600, reflecting higher home prices and more competition. The Northeast also sees the largest gap between what buyers are paying as a down payment today compared to pre-pandemic.

Compared to 2019, the Northeast has seen down payments climb 236.8%, significantly more than the next closest gap of 134.0% in the Midwest. These trends are consistent with the persistent upward pressure on home prices in these regions as scarce inventory is met with sustained buyer demand.

Get ready for some good news. There are a lot of misconceptions about who qualifies for down payment assistance.

“Many people think these programs are only available to low-income borrowers, first-time homebuyers, or for properties that have sales price limits,” says Down Payment Resource's Khandelwal. “But if you look, you’ll find specialized programs designed to assist specific groups, including first-generation homebuyers, minorities, Indigenous people, people of color, veterans, those with government jobs, disabilities, and more.”

Here’s something else to smile about: A first-time homebuyer doesn't just mean someone who's never bought a home before.

The federal government generally holds a broader definition of a first-time homebuyer. It’s someone who has not been a homeowner in the past three years. If you sold a house three-and-a-half years ago, you qualify as first-time buyer.

Buyers can take several different steps to find a down payment assistance program that’s right for them.

Check the federal programs mentioned above (like HUD, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac), and see if there’s anything suitable.

Buyers should also visit their state’s Department of Housing website and see what might be listed, or call their number and inquire what down payment assistance programs might be available. Cities, towns, private lenders, and nonprofits may also have help.

“Homebuyers should seek the assistance of a mortgage lender who specializes in affordable lending to identify their best options,” advises Khandelwal.

In terms of what is typically needed to access aid, the documentation is very much in line with what’s needed to apply for any mortgage. Buyers will likely need the following:

Pay stubs plus W-2s from the past few years to verify employment and income history

Details on the property they intend to buy (The real estate agent can share this information.)

The paperwork is processed in much the same way as a home loan, and there may be requests for more documents.

Then, if buyers are approved, they will be ready to move ahead with a lower—or no—down payment as their homeownership journey unfolds.

Janet Siroto is a journalist, editor, and trend tracker. Her work has appeared in Cosmopolitan, Good Housekeeping, and other publications.

#5596. Home Prices Hold Steady as Sales Drop and Inventory Expands

Home prices remained relatively resilient in October despite a sharp slowdown in sales and continued growth in available inventory.

The national median sale price was $383,598, down 0.4% from October 2025, according to the latest housing market analysis from Homes.com. Home sales fell 11.7% year over year while inventory increased 4.8%.

The combination gave buyers more choices even as elevated mortgage rates limited demand while sellers faced greater competition for the smaller pool of buyers prepared to purchase.

“October’s results tell a more nuanced story than the nearly flat national price number alone would suggest,” says Brad Case, chief residential economist at Homes.com. “Sales were down substantially from a year ago even as buyers had more homes to choose from, yet prices barely moved. That suggests demand remains strong, but buyers appear increasingly selective about which homes they choose to purchase.”

Single-family homes posted the smallest annual price decline among the property types tracked by Homes.com. The median price declined 0.3% from October 2025, compared with 1.4% declines for both townhomes and condominiums.

Single-family sales fell 11.2% year over year, while inventory increased 5%. Townhome sales dropped 13.5% as inventory grew 5.3%, and condo sales fell 15.1% while inventory increased 3.6%.

The figures point to a market where additional inventory has yet to translate into significant national price declines, particularly for single-family homes, Homes.com points out.

The relatively flat national median masks significant differences among major housing markets. Among the 40 largest markets tracked, 10 posted annual price gains of at least 2%, while nine recorded declines of 2% or more.

San Francisco posted the largest highlighted gain, with its median sale price rising 17.7% year over year despite a 13% decline in sales. Jacksonville prices increased 6.1% even as sales fell 14.4%. On the opposite hand, Austin recorded a 9.7% annual price decline, followed by a 4.1% decrease in Nashville.

Inventory trends also varied widely. Seattle had 22.8% more homes for sale than a year earlier, while inventory in Jacksonville was 9.8% lower.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5595. Compass, MLSs Jockey Over Jurisdictions as Lawsuits Sprawl

In the ongoing legal battle between Compass and more than a dozen large MLSs across the country, both sides are maneuvering to control how and where the cases are tried, as the mega-brokerage seeks to spread the litigation as widely as possible.

The Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), one of 15 MLSs sued by Compass last week, filed a letter with the Southern District of New York on Nov. 18, arguing that Compass’s motion to “splinter one dispute across multiple courts” should be denied.

“Compass’s effort to scatter this dispute across multiple courts would create unnecessary complexity and expense without changing the fundamental issue at stake,” said Jeff Bosch, CEO of Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service, in a statement shared with RISMedia. “We are defending cooperation rules that promote fair competition, give buyers broader access to available homes, and help sellers reach more potential buyers. We believe these rules are lawful and procompetitive, and we look forward to defending them in court.”

Simultaneously, Compass is grappling with court rules that require it to notify judges of related cases as it pursues a larger goal of maximizing pressure on each MLS, arguing that the lawsuits should proceed separately despite their many similarities.

“The overlap between the cases concerning the subject of the challenged rules and Compass’s phased-marketing program does not justify coordinating cases that involve different defendants, markets, witnesses, and damages,” Compass wrote in a letter filed in the Southern District of California.

The back-and-forth is the latest key maneuver as Compass and the MLSs battle over rules that prevent pre-marketed or off-MLS listings from being shown on the MLS.

As the mega-brokerage pursues a broad campaign to remake real estate, it has not shied away from using its significant size and resources to lean on MLSs that have stuck to their policies (specifically, restrictions on off-MLS marketing). In a September letter sent to the MLSs it would eventually sue, Compass explicitly pointed to the legal costs of defending a lawsuit, and promised to spend “millions of dollars to sue” MLSs that defied it.

In at least three of its lawsuits targeting MLSs, Compass informed federal judges of the other two-dozen lawsuits it has filed, while simultaneously arguing those lawsuits should not be consolidated or reassigned, claiming “each case turns on a distinct defendant, rule, and local market.”

Still, Compass acknowledged that the cases “overlap…in a limited respect,” but wrote in one letter it would not “concede…that consolidation, coordination, reassignment, or transfer would be appropriate.”

With around 350,000 federal civil lawsuits filed every year, judges are often highly motivated to find efficiencies and avoid redundancies in their caseloads. To that end, many districts require that attorneys notify the court of cases with similar factual elements or common parties filed in other districts, allowing judges to coordinate, consolidate or otherwise smooth out the litigation process.

In one of its letters, Compass cited this rule but said it was only informing the judge out of “an abundance of caution,” while still arguing the the other lawsuits “do not arise from the same or substantially identical transactions, happenings, or events.”

Forcing each MLS to defend a separate lawsuit will likely increase litigation costs overall, with Compass better able to bear that burden as a well-funded public company. At the same time, judges are also likely to consider geographic factors, as any consolidated case would force some MLSs to travel further for proceedings.

On November 12, Compass sued 15 MLSs in 15 separate actions in 11 districts, claiming their longstanding broker cooperation rules violated antitrust law. The en masse filing was preceded by a letter Compass sent to several MLSs in September, warning them to cease enforcement of their broker cooperation rules or face federal antitrust claims.

In response, six MLSs, later joined by one more, filed a lawsuit in New York seeking to prevent Compass from suing them along with a declaration that their cooperation rules are lawful under federal antitrust laws (and state-law analogues).

The MLSs have also sought to rally together, with at least two separate legal defense funds in the works—one by CRMLS, and another through the Council of Multiple Listing Services (which has not been named in the litigation, though many of the targeted MLSs are members).

In its November 13 motion, Compass claimed that the action filed by the MLSs should either be dismissed or handled individually in the jurisdictions where each MLS resides.

ARMLS counsel Gregory S. Skidmore argued in his letter that trying the cases individually would create “massive inefficiencies and duplication of effort.”

“The MLS Parties sued Compass where it is headquartered, and where Compass itself has chosen to litigate its own Cooperation Rules–related suit,” wrote Skidmore, referring to the brokerage’s injunction hearing against Zillow in November of 2025. “Compass has not shown any ‘indication that nonparty witnesses would refuse to appear’…and Compass’s executives reside in New York,” he continued. “Nor is any other district the locus of operative facts: Compass’s campaign originated at its New York headquarters and reached nationwide.”

Compass, in its separate letters, argued that each case is more about the local circumstances and specific rules of each MLS, and directly disputed that consolidation would create more efficiencies, and noted that potential damages will depend on sales prices in local real estate markets.

Skidmore, on the other hand, urged the SDNY court to to focus on “judicial economy” and claiming that Compass “bears the burden” of showing that severing the case is necessary.

“Transfer would create seven suits in five districts, each replicating Compass’s evidence,” he added. “Courts need not indulge an ‘onslaught of litigation.'”

Maria Patterson is the Executive Vice President and Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5594. Hosting Guests Is Reshaping What Americans Want in a Home

Hosting friends and family may be doing more than filling the house. It’s also changing the way Americans think about what they want from their homes.

A new survey commissioned by KB Home found 58% of Americans say hosting guests has made them rethink what they want in their current or future home. The research, conducted by Talker Research, surveyed 2,000 U.S. adults in October.

Gathering spaces emerged as particularly important when respondents considered what makes a home comfortable for holiday hosting and special occasions. Open living areas led the list, selected by 35% of Americans, followed by outdoor entertaining spaces at 30%.

Kitchens also figured prominently. Twenty-four percent prioritized a spacious kitchen, while 21% selected an open kitchen. Another 21% pointed to a large or dedicated dining space.

“Hosting friends and family can highlight what people love about their homes and what they wish worked better,” says Gena Kirk, vice president of corporate design at KB Home. “From spacious living areas and open floor plans to finishes that reflect personal style, a KB home works for everyday life as well as special occasions.”

Having guests over also appears to sharpen homeowners’ perceptions of their existing spaces.

Nearly one-third of hosts, 31%, said entertaining makes them think about ways to make their homes more welcoming or comfortable, and 25% said it makes them want to declutter or clean more often.

The experience isn’t always positive. While 29% of hosts said entertaining makes them feel proud of their homes, 20% said it makes them self-conscious and 24% notice things they would like to change.

Shared spaces receive much of that scrutiny before guests arrive. Among hosts, 45% said they focus most on tidying the living room, followed by bathrooms at 35% and kitchens at 31%.

For builders, the findings reinforce the continued importance of flexible gathering spaces that can serve both everyday life and larger get-togethers. They also point to the role kitchens, outdoor areas, and living rooms play not simply as individual rooms but as interconnected entertaining spaces.

Talker Research conducted the online survey for KB Home between Oct. 9 and Oct. 13 among 2,000 U.S. adults with internet access.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5591. Single-Family Starts Rise 4% as Permits Drop in October

Single-family housing starts rebounded in October, but a drop in permitting activity suggests builders remain cautious about new construction heading into the end of the year.

Single-family starts increased 4% from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 864,000, according to the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and Department of Housing and Urban Development. September’s single-family starts rate was revised to 831,000.

Overall, privately owned housing starts increased 9.9% from September to an annual rate of 1.309 million. The October pace was 2.8% above the October 2025 rate of 1.273 million.

Permitting activity moved in the opposite direction during October. Single-family permits fell 8.7% from the prior month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September. Overall building permits declined 7.4% month over month and 8.7% year over year to an annual rate of 1.295 million. Permits for buildings with five or more units were at a rate of 475,000.

Single-family completions also gained ground in October, rising 6.3% from September to an annual rate of 900,000, compared with a revised 847,000 the previous month.

#5590. Despite posting a solid earnings beat, Elastic sees its stock slide on rough guidance

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

The company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

However, investors were less than impressed with the company’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

Netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The company also sells application observability and security tools.

In the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the company has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

Elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) said he’s excited about the potential of those new capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”

Unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the company published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

Elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

Elastic is trying to sidestep those concerns by de-emphasizing search and observability and moving towards runtime context, model evaluation and AI operations, but investors are not yet convinced it will be able to do so successfully, Constellation Research analyst Michael Ni told SiliconANGLE.

“While Elastic is showing good underlying momentum, the Street wants to see more proof that its re-acceleration can hold,” Ni said. “The next few quarters will show whether the broader platform story translates into sustainable growth or remains ahead of the numbers.”

#5589. How Bedroom Counts Vary Across Rental Products in Growth Markets

Rental housing encompasses a range of product types, each offering different configurations and levels of space. Across major growth markets, bedroom counts provide one way to understand how these products differ and where they may compete for renters.

Zonda’s third-quarter 2026 Rental Housing Outlook examined bedroom counts across cottages, townhomes, higher-density detached homes, and single-family rentals in major housing markets.

Single-family rentals generally offered the most bedrooms, while cottages tended to offer the fewest. Beyond that pattern, individual markets revealed notable differences in how rental products were configured, providing additional context for builders and developers assessing their competitive landscape.

Among the markets analyzed, Salt Lake City had the highest average bedroom count for single-family rentals, at 4.8 bedrooms. That is nearly two bedrooms more than the market’s average townhome rental, highlighting the differences in space offered across rental products within the same market.

Charlotte also ranked near the top for average bedrooms in single-family rentals, while San Antonio sat at the other end of the spectrum.

These differences can also influence how rental properties compete with for-sale housing. Larger single-family rentals may appeal to households that might otherwise consider purchasing a home, while smaller cottages and townhomes may attract renters with different space needs.

Single-family rentals, however, are only part of the story, with market rankings shifting across other rental product types.

Tampa led the analyzed markets for bedroom counts in higher-density detached rentals, while Orlando stood out for townhomes. San Antonio, despite having the lowest average bedroom count for single-family rentals among the markets studied, had the highest cottage average. Nashville sat at the opposite end of the cottage comparison.

These variations highlight the importance of looking beyond overall rental inventory when evaluating a market. Understanding the mix of rental products and the space they offer can provide additional context for builders and developers assessing local competition.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s Rental Housing Outlook subscription.

They’re still business partners, however, and are set to open a new hair salon together in Miami.

“We are continuing to grow our brand together, even though we are separated,” she said.

Katsanevas and Trujillo currently operate nine locations of their business, Lunatic Fringe Salon, across Utah, Ohio, and Idaho.

While she’s focused on remaining positive, Katsanevas said it took some time to work through the complicated feelings that accompanied the change.

“It does take a minute to mourn the loss of the way your life once was and what it looked like,” she said. “I’ve processed, I’ve cried, I’ve accepted. I’ve had to swim away from the muddy waters to get to the clear water and say, ‘OK, I’m coming out of this and I’m going to be OK.’”

#5586. New-Home Sales Drop 11.7% as Market Slips Into Underperformance

New-home market conditions weakened further in October as declining buyer traffic, softer sales, and persistent affordability pressures weighed on builders.

Zonda’s National Market Ranking fell to 87.4, moving the new-home market into “slightly underperforming” territory. Sales declined 3.1% from September and 11.7% from a year earlier, a significantly steeper annual decline than September’s 4.6% drop.

Zonda’s October builder sentiment survey also pointed to softer conditions. Eighty-six percent of builders reported slower-than-expected demand, up from 84% in September. Builders cited declining traffic, limited buyer urgency, and growing frustration with the effectiveness of incentives.

“One of the biggest challenges for builders right now is generating enough buyer interest in the first place,” says Sarah Bonnarens, director of economic research for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Builders still have an advantage when it comes to pricing and financing flexibility, but those tools can only do so much when buyer traffic is down. The challenge is keeping sales moving without putting even more pressure on margins.”

Zonda reported a seasonally adjusted annualized sales rate of 638,568 new homes in October, down 3.1% month over month and 11.7% year over year. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 50,770 homes were sold, 11.6% fewer than a year earlier and 2.8% below October 2019.

Incentives remained a prominent feature of the market. Sixty-four percent of new-home communities advertised incentives on to-be-built homes, while 83% offered incentives on quick move-in inventory. Zonda notes the figures include only publicly available incentives and therefore underrepresent overall usage.

The New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) registered 122.8 in October, down 11.4% from the same month last year and 29.5% below its cycle high. On a monthly basis, seasonally adjusted new-home sales measured by the index decreased 1.9%.

All of Zonda’s select markets posted year-over-year PSI declines. Minneapolis held up best, declining 0.3%, followed by Charlotte at 1.1%, and Tampa at 3.5%. The steepest declines occurred in Los Angeles/Orange County at 31.4%, Riverside/San Bernardino at 28.4%, and Denver at 26.3%.

Price reductions also became more common as builders worked to maintain sales pace. Forty-three percent of builders surveyed by Zonda lowered prices in October, up from 38% in September. Another 54% held prices flat, while just 3% increased them. In September, 10% of builders reported raising prices.

Entry-level home prices declined 2.6% year over year to $316,019, while move-up prices slipped 0.5% to $515,075. High-end prices increased 2.7% to $951,036. Zonda says the high-end increase partly reflects new communities opening at higher price points with larger homesites, bigger floor plans, and more desirable locations.

Zonda tracked 18,159 actively selling communities in October, up 6.7% from a year earlier and 0.6% from September. Community count remained 5.9% below the same month in 2019.

Quick move-in inventory (QMI) totaled 38,602 homes nationwide, up 8.6% year over year but down 3.3% month over month. QMI supply remained 72.3% above 2019 levels. There were 2.3 quick move-in homes per community nationally, about even with the same period last year.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5585. What Retirement Buyers Want From Their Next Home, According to PulteGroup

Warm weather remains a major draw for retirement-age home buyers considering a move, but a new PulteGroup survey suggests the decision is becoming about more than just climate.

The survey of 1,330 prospective home buyers at or nearing retirement age found differences between what working and already-retired respondents prioritize when considering an out-of-state move. Among those still working, 62% selected weather and climate as one of their top two reasons to relocate, while 47% cited affordability and cost of living, and 35% selected proximity to family or friends.

For respondents who were already retired, family connections carried more weight. Forty-five percent selected proximity to family or friends, tying weather and climate as their leading considerations for moving out of state.

“For many buyers, retirement isn’t just about where they want to live, but how they want to live,” said Sean Strickler, president of PulteGroup’s West Florida division and brand champion for Explore by Del Webb. “Warm weather will always have its appeal, but buyers are also thinking about how their next home will support the lifestyle they envision, whether that’s spending more time with family, building friendships, or enjoying new experiences.”

When respondents were asked what they prioritized in their next home, 59% selected a low-maintenance lifestyle, making it the most commonly cited consideration. Affordability and financial peace of mind followed at 48%, while 39% selected luxurious, resort-style amenities.

The findings show that builders targeting active-adult and retirement buyers may need to balance amenity-rich communities with homes that reduce the day-to-day responsibilities associated with homeownership.

Community programming also ranked prominently. When asked what matters most in selecting their next community, 62% chose built-in activities, social opportunities, and a sense of community. Safety and peace of mind followed at 42%, while 40% selected proximity to quality health care.

Those priorities align with expectations for retirement itself. Nearly half of respondents, 48%, said they were looking forward to more travel and new experiences, while the same share cited a stronger social life and sense of community. And 96% expect their next home to be where they spend their retirement years.

Family proximity extended beyond respondents already in retirement. Among all surveyed prospective buyers who have children, 74% said proximity to children or grandchildren was either the primary reason or an important factor in where they would purchase their next home.

The Southeast continues to stand out among respondents contemplating an out-of-state move. Florida was the leading destination, selected by 25%, followed by South Carolina at 19%, and North Carolina at 17%. Together, the three states accounted for 61% of potential destinations selected by respondents considering relocation.

The preferences overlap with PulteGroup’s expansion of its active-adult and lifestyle offerings in the region. The company has more than 80 active Del Webb and DiVosta communities in Florida and recently launched a Panhandle division. It is also developing two Tampa-area communities under its Explore by Del Webb brand.

In the Carolinas, PulteGroup has additional projects underway, including the 670-acre Carolina Ridge near Charlotte and the 500-acre Del Webb Point Hope near Charleston.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5584. Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion Valuation Exceeds the Worth of Every Home in San Francisco

Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the company’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.

The Claude developer, which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range. The company sold 980 million Class A shares, raising an initial $81 billion and shattering SpaceX’s $72 billion record.

To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate—and the statistics are shocking.

San Francisco is a longtime hot spot for tech giants. It saw the growth of Google and Facebook, and has now become the landing spot for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI startups. The constant stream of tech wealth, combined with a limited number of desirable homes, has created a competitive market. San Francisco County has a median sales price of $1.6 million, and yet, Anthropic blows the entire market out of the water.

The aggregate value of every home for sale in San Francisco is a mere $8.6 billion, a small fraction of Anthropic's new valuation. Indeed, the total value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metro is $1.37 trillion, according to the 2-25 American Community Survey. Anthropic’s valuation exceeds that by about $123 billion.

This trend is consistent in 391 metros out of 393.

The only two metros with more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth are New York City, at $3.26 trillion, and Los Angeles, at $2.64 trillion.

Furthermore, the AI giant’s valuation tops the owner-occupied home value in 46 out of the 50 states, as well as Washington, DC.

The value of all owner-occupied homes in the state of New Jersey comes in at $1.44 trillion, just shy of Anthropic’s valuation.

Throughout the country, all owner-occupied homes are worth $43.6 trillion. Anthropic’s valuation equals about 3.4% of all owner-occupied housing wealth in the United States.

When it comes to homes on the market, Anthropic’s valuation stacks up high.

Across the U.S., about 1.18 million homes are for sale, listed for a combined $816 billion. Anthropic’s valuation could snap up every single one and still have $678 billion left.

Even without the first $1 trillion of the valuation, the remaining $494 billion could buy every home for sale in the 20 metros with the highest total listing value with billions to spare: about 372,000 homes listed at a combined $356 billion.

As Anthropic’s debut is discussed, the valuation may be rounded to $1.49 trillion, as it’s common for financial figures to be kept to one or two digits. However, that dropped digit in the $1.494 trillion figure is $4 billion. That rounding error alone is greater than the combined value of every owner-occupied home in Racine, WI, which total $3.97 billion.

That same $4 billion could buy every home for sale in Alaska: 2,196 listings worth $1.16 billion. For a change in scenery, it could then cover every home for sale on Kauai, the Kapa’a, Hawaii, market, which has 356 listings worth $925 million, and still have about $1.9 billion left to purchase all the homes for sale in the Boulder, CO, metro area.

It’s no wonder the AI boom is reshaping markets in tech hubs like New York City and San Francisco, when the valuation of just one company looms so high.

#5583. Building-Permit Woes Tip Leading Economic Indicators Negative

Leading economic indicators for the month of October took a slight downturn, as the latest Leading Economic Index (LEI) report from business research organization The Conference Board recorded a 0.3% drop to 99.3 from September.

The LEI is a predictive tool designed to anticipate the direction of the economy in the coming months. It is based on 10 component indicators, which, for example, include measures of average consumer expectations and the average weekly initial claims of unemployment insurance.

Justyna Zabinska-La Monica, senior manager of Business Cycle Indicators at The Conference Board, said that “The US LEI’s decline in October was mostly fueled by fewer building permits.”

Recent data on building permits has indeed been dismal. This month’s New Residential Construction report, for example, showed that permits were down 7.4% month-over-month and 8.7% year-over-year.

Zabinska-La Monica, for her part, emphasized that “(b)uilding permits data were at the weakest level since May 2020…Compared to September and one year ago, permits declined across all categories, including by type of dwelling and region. The only exception was the Midwest, where total permits were up slightly since September and 8.1% over the last 12 months.”

Zabinska-La Monica also singled out “consumer expectations for business conditions, average hours worked in manufacturing, and manufacturers’ new orders for nondefense capital goods” as “negative contributors” to October’s LEI. “Weakness in these components more than offset gains in others,” she explained.

The other two major indices in The Conference Board’s report, the Coincident Economic Index (CEI) and Lagging Economic Index (LAG), were both unchanged (apart from some minor September data revisions mentioned in the report).

The CEI, in contrast to the LEI, is considered a summary of indicators on the current state of the economy. The LAG serves as an after-the-fact confirmation of the state of the economy.

The overall outlook of The Conference Board, despite some disheartening October data, is still seemingly positive. Zabinska-La Monica noted that “the LEI’s six-month growth rate remained positive,” which “indicat(es) continued economic expansion ahead.” This economic expansion, however, will be “increasingly investment-led with softer household demand.”

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5582. Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently launched AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business users. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.
