#5472. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5470. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:

First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:

The first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

As seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer says deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision.  At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

Google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

Now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

That said, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:

Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

Coming back to the AI inference issue. As we showed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract says.”

This means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

For sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

In this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:

We see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

This means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

For vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

Sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

#5469. Stablecoin Market Loses Billions: Where Is Crypto’s Liquidity Going?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

The contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap shows that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

CryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

The current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

That monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

This time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

#5468. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

An EHR Built Around Allergy. Now, With AI at Its Core.

The objective is to reduce repetitive administrative work while keeping essential front-office processes connected.

ModuleMDQâ¢ adds another dimension through conversational practice intelligence. Instead of navigating multiple screens to locate information, practice teams can interact with their practice data using natural language and get answers that help them move work forward.

Together, these capabilities reflect a broader direction for the ModuleMD EHR: clinical workflows, administrative operations and practice intelligence working as one system.

#5466. Rene Haas to Take Over Nvidia? What Will Happen to Crypto?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Nvidia could be about to hand its biggest job to the man who helped turn Arm into one of the world’s most valuable chip companies. Rene Haas is now being considered as a potential successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia, a familiar face at the center of the AI industry’s biggest leadership change.

Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s recruitment firm had approached Haas as part of its search for a new chief executive. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

Rene Haas has been approached regarding the CEO role at Nvidia by recruiting firm Heidrick & Struggles, which was hired by the board to replace Jensen Huang https://t.co/yiJ6NkvEtS

An appointment would put someone with experience at both companies in charge of Nvidia’s next chapter. But what does it mean for crypto? Could Haas push the AI boom even further, and what would that mean for Bitcoin and the rest of the market?

Haas is not an outsider to Nvidia. He previously ran the company’s computing products business between 2006 and 2013, giving him direct experience with the company before its transformation into an AI powerhouse.

His subsequent run at Arm offers a glimpse of what he might bring to the role. Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for its fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. Its profit before tax climbed from $756 million to $960 million. The company has also moved beyond its traditional chip-design licensing business, introducing its own AGI CPU for AI data centers in March 2026.

Arm’s technology already reaches more than 99% of smartphones sold worldwide. Its designs also power computing infrastructure used by major cloud providers and Nvidia itself.

Haas helped position the company for a much larger role in the AI economy. Now, his next challenge could be taking Nvidia beyond selling the chips powering that expansion.

Nvidia’s existing business gives him an enormous starting point. The company generated $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue in its latest results, with data center sales accounting for $107.6 billion. Revenue increased 103% from a year earlier.

Its next-generation Vera Rubin platform has also entered production and begun shipping. A new CEO would inherit an extraordinary growth engine, but also the responsibility of deciding how aggressively Nvidia should expand its influence across the AI industry.

If Haas brings his Arm strategy to Nvidia, we could see a push into integrated computing platforms, data center infrastructure and new AI applications. That could create another wave of investment across the technology sector.

Crypto could benefit if Haas turns Nvidia’s next chapter into another catalyst for AI infrastructure spending. The connection extends beyond tokens carrying artificial intelligence branding. Bitcoin and Ethereum have increasingly moved in tandem with technology stocks during periods when investors shift between risk assets.

A stronger Nvidia could help restore confidence in the AI investment cycle, especially if investors believe its leadership transition will not interrupt infrastructure spending.

Decentralized computing projects such as Render, Bittensor, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, and Akash could also benefit. These networks are trying to capture demand for GPU resources, distributed computing, and AI development.

More spending on AI infrastructure would create opportunities for decentralized alternatives. Developers need computing power, and centralized providers cannot always meet every requirement at the right price.

The bigger opportunity could come from investor appetite rather than immediate demand for crypto tokens. If Nvidia shares regain momentum under Rene Haas, technology investors could become more comfortable taking risks elsewhere. That would give crypto a potential source of buying interest.

Haas has already demonstrated what he can do with Arm. Taking over Nvidia would give him a considerably larger platform, with consequences extending well beyond semiconductor stocks.

#5463. ‘The bottleneck used to be dumpling-folding talent’: Din Tai Fung CEO on America’s top-grossing restaurant chain turning craft into corporate training

The restaurant chain with the highest per-store sales in America says the thing that used to limit its growth was a labor shortage of a very specific kind. Anyone who’s had the soup dumplings at the memorable chain can attest to seeing the lab-coated technicians behind the glass windows working their magic.

“The bottleneck used to be dumpling-folding talent,” Albert Yang, CEO of Din Tai Fung North America, told Fortune by email. “But through continuous improvements to our training programs, we’ve largely overcome that challenge.”

Dumpling-folding talent is a phrase with a lot of history behind it. For most of the time Chinese food has been sold in America, the people folding it were family: the owner, the spouse, the kids and, as Lucas Sin, chef at the New York chain Junzi Kitchen, put it in a 2020 Fortune roundtable, “a cousin of a cousin of a cousin from Fujian.”

At Din Tai Fung, folding is now a corporate job track: a 12-week training program, and a dumpling training manager in every U.S. restaurant, Yang told the Los Angeles Times in 2023.

That swap, from family labor to systems, is reshaping Chinese food in America. Din Tai Fung’s U.S. restaurants averaged $27.4 million in sales in 2024, nearly double the next-closest chain, according to Technomic data reported by Restaurant Business. Panda Express, co-run by an engineer who built her own point-of-sale system in the 1980s, now tops $6 billion a year.

The old Chinese-American restaurant, as the people who ran it describe it, depended on cheap labor at the start and a ready buyer at the end.

Foreign Policy reported in 2019 the waves of migrants from rural Fujian, who had staffed takeout kitchens in the 1980s and 1990s had died down as living conditions in China improved. Wages for takeout cooks had climbed from about $1,500 a month in the 1980s to close to $4,000. The family side ran out too. A 2019 New York Times analysis of Yelp data found Chinese restaurants fell from 7.3% to 6.5% of all restaurants across the 20 largest U.S. metro areas over five years, about 1,200 fewer places, as owners retired and their college-educated kids took other jobs.

“There was no succession plan, because success was seen as not having to do it anymore,” Jason Wang, cofounder of Xi’an Famous Foods, said in the Fortune roundtable.

The pressure hasn’t eased. In 2025, chain restaurant sales grew at their slowest pace outside the pandemic since the Great Recession, and Restaurant Business listed an immigration crackdown among the reasons, along with weak consumer confidence, weight-loss drugs and bad weather, in its Technomic Top 500 coverage.

Yang tells the demand side through his own childhood. Many Americans, he said, first met Chinese food at cheap fast-food and fast-casual spots opened by immigrants who couldn’t afford beautiful dining rooms.

“They were focused on surviving, supporting their families, and building a future for the next generation,” he said.

But now, the Chinese food offered by his family’s company is downright aspirational.

“I remember growing up, my mom would pack me Chinese food for lunch, and other kids would sometimes make fun of me for it,” he said. “Now, I hear from parents that their kids actually think it’s cool when someone brings leftover Din Tai Fung to school for lunch.”

Din Tai Fung was inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame this month as a “Global Family Legacy” honoree; Albert and Aaron Yang accepted on behalf of the family at the Nov. 5 ceremony in Los Angeles.

The Chinese food businesses that have scaled in America are the ones that replaced family labor with process early.

Panda Express is a top example. Andrew Cherng’s family opened Panda Inn in Pasadena in 1973, and business was so slow at first his mother would sprinkle salt on the threshold to chase off evil spirits, he said at Nation’s Restaurant News’ CREATE conference in July. His wife, Peggy Cherng, is an engineer by training. When point-of-sale systems barely existed in the mid-1980s, she built one.

“We had to develop it ourselves,” she said. Panda now has more than 2,600 U.S. locations, more than $6 billion in annual sales, and its own Panda University for employees—ranking it 11th among U.S. chains.

People in the business saw this coming years ago.

“Automation and central kitchens will take over,” Wong of the culinary federation told Foreign Policy in 2019. Zhao predicted takeouts would be consolidated under new brands that keep prices low through automation.

The newest arrivals come with systems already built. Chinese chains including HeyTea, Chagee, Luckin Coffee, Wallace, and Haidilao, some with thousands of stores at home, have pushed into U.S. cities to escape a price war in a saturated home market, the Times reported in December 2025.

“China’s food service industry is suffering from severe oversupply,” Bob Qing, founder of the restaurant investor Tomato Capital, told the paper. Limited-service Asian and noodle chains grew U.S. sales 7.8% in 2025, faster than any other segment, according to Technomic data reported by Restaurant Business.

Din Tai Fung is the cleanest example, because its whole product is the thing that’s hardest to systematize. Each Din Tai Fung restaurant turns out about 10,000 dumplings a day with roughly 30 chefs on rotation, each dumpling held to 18 folds and 21 grams, the LA Times reported in 2023. Kan Kuang-Ming, the chain’s head chef in Taiwan, told the paper: “You have to fail about 1,400 times before you can make one that is beautiful.”

In Taiwan, new chefs learn by shadowing a senior chef. In the U.S., they go through a training program instead.

“Our current training program is 12 weeks, though it still takes six months and up to a year to get up to speed,” Albert Yang told the Times then. Entry-level hourly jobs started at $20 an hour, he said, and managers at $100,000.

The family business started the old way. Founder Bing-Yi Yang opened a cooking oil shop in Taipei in 1958, according to Restaurant Business, and later hired a Shanghai-born chef to make soup dumplings, the LA Times reported. When his son Frank opened the first U.S. location in Arcadia, Calif., in 2000, the grandsons worked the register.

“We were running credit cards when we could barely even see over the counter,” Aaron Yang told the paper.

Albert Yang now says the system is far enough along to speed up. Din Tai Fung opened three U.S. restaurants this year, in Irvine and Brea, Calif., and Scottsdale, Ariz. Yang credited years of spending on the company’s people, leadership development, training programs, operational systems and production capabilities.

Asked about a ceiling, he told Fortune: “I don’t believe in setting an arbitrary limit.”

The constraint he names now is the company’s own standards.

“Today, our bottleneck isn’t necessarily a physical or operational constraint,” he said. “It’s a self-imposed one driven by the quality standards we’re unwilling to compromise.” The other is real estate: A Din Tai Fung typically needs 10,000 to 20,000 square feet, which he called “incredibly challenging” to find in a prime spot in Manhattan or Brooklyn.

But for New Yorkers who had to wait many years before the first location opened in the Broadway district, in the former Mars 2112 space, the wait is already ending for location number two: The next one is set for Downtown Brooklyn, where Din Tai Fung has signed for 20,000 square feet in The Brook, a 52-story tower at 567 Fulton St., scheduled to open in 2027, according to the Brooklyn Paper.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5462. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5461. XRP Has an Institutional Edge, But Garlinghouse Believes Wall Street Is Pulling Liquidity Away

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

The XRP price is struggling to take advantage of institutional credibility for the ledger. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has another explanation: Wall Street is pulling liquidity toward blockbuster IPOs.

The XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

This makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

The XRP Ledger Foundation has completed the attestation of the XRP Ledger against the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. It is the first public, permissionless layer-1 blockchain to have the toolkit's Architecture and Resiliency principles independently… pic.twitter.com/wEKczeEdrF

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

CertiK said it reviewed all 112 controls in the toolkit. Its technical verification focused on those suitable for independent assessment. The firm also verified Partior’s self-attestation under the same two principles.

Institutional adoption of digital assets depends on trust backed by independent verification and evidence.CertiK has completed independent technical verification of @XRPLF’s and Partior’s self-attestations under the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit,… pic.twitter.com/nQoEXjDHLh

The XRPL Foundation called it the first such verification for a public, permissionless Layer 1. The milestone gives institutions a structured reference when evaluating networks for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, funds, and other assets.

That is useful progress for XRPL’s institutional pitch. Risk and compliance teams can now examine evidence against familiar market-infrastructure standards. They have more than a blockchain’s own description of its capabilities.

In the interview, Garlinghouse addressed the gap between Ripple’s expansion and XRP price performance. He said the SpaceX IPO triggered a similar pullback as investors shifted liquidity out of crypto. He specifically named Bitcoin and XRP among the assets affected.

Investors moved capital from liquid crypto markets into the highly anticipated SpaceX listing, he said. Garlinghouse sees the same pattern ahead of Anthropic’s debut.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday. The offering covers 980 million shares, and the deal is expected to close Friday, November 20.

“What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets,” Garlinghouse said. “I think you’ll see that happen here as well.”

He also expects digital assets to stop moving in lockstep. In his view, real utility and demand will increasingly separate stronger projects from speculative tokens. That puts the XRP price debate back on XRPL’s ability to attract activity.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin Hyper is chasing a similar infrastructure opportunity as XRPL, this time around Bitcoin. Its Layer 2 combines Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) technology with Bitcoin settlement, aiming to bring faster transactions, DeFi applications, and staking to the Bitcoin ecosystem.

The project has already rolled out its public testnet, explorer, wallet, faucet, bridge, and staking portal. These releases give developers and early users a working environment to explore before the planned mainnet rollout.

The presale has raised more than $33.2 million, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136. The November 26 deadline is now approaching, leaving less than a week before the scheduled presale close.

XRPL’s latest institutional milestone shows how infrastructure improvements can strengthen a blockchain’s appeal to financial players. Bitcoin Hyper is pursuing a different route, building an execution layer that could make Bitcoin more useful across payments and decentralized finance.

If Bitcoin Layer 2 adoption gains traction, projects delivering faster execution and financial applications could attract growing institutional attention. Bitcoin Hyper is positioning itself ahead of that opportunity, with its presale entering its final stretch.

#5460. Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin Explains When a Business Needs a Fractional CIO

Lionel Fermin examines when growing businesses may need technology leadership for planning, security, spending, and long-term technology decisions.

HOBBS, N.M., Nov. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When does a business need a Fractional CIO? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin of GlobaTech Solutions in Hobbs, New Mexico, explains when businesses may benefit from experienced technology leadership.

The HelloNation article explains that technology decisions often become more complicated as a business grows. New employees, software, equipment, and security risks can create challenges that basic technical support may not address. At that point, business leaders may need broader guidance about how technology supports the organization.

The article describes a Fractional CIO as someone who provides technology leadership without serving as a full-time executive. While technical support typically focuses on fixing problems and keeping systems working, this role considers how technology decisions affect employees, customers, security, costs, and future business needs.

This broader perspective can become important when several technology projects compete for attention. The article notes that businesses may recognize the need for improvements without knowing which ones should come first. Fractional CIO services can help prioritize projects according to risk, cost, and business value.

Technology planning is another major part of the role. Instead of waiting for systems or equipment to fail, the article explains that companies can prepare for equipment replacements, software changes, security improvements, and growth. Identifying major expenses early can also give leaders more time to compare options and prepare budgets.

Cybersecurity can create another need for technology leadership. The article notes that a security incident can interrupt operations, create financial losses, and affect customer relationships. Executive technology guidance can help leaders understand cybersecurity risks in business terms and determine which concerns deserve the most attention.

The article also describes how Fractional CIO services can assist with customer or industry security requirements. Businesses may receive questionnaires or requests to demonstrate specific protections. Technology leadership can help identify gaps, organize responses, and provide a clearer view of existing security practices.

Growth can also signal the need for more structured technology guidance. Systems that worked for a small team may become strained as a company adds employees. The article explains that a technology strategy can help businesses prepare for greater demands on software, networks, security, and employee access.

Vendor management is another area where stronger oversight may be useful. Companies often work with separate providers for software, internet service, phones, security, and technical support. The article notes that reviewing vendor costs, contracts, performance, and responsibilities can help reduce duplication and clarify who handles important technology needs.

Major business changes can also increase the need for planning. Opening a new office, replacing software, or hiring many employees may require coordination among leadership, employees, vendors, and technical teams. Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin's insights featured in the article address how technology leadership can help keep these decisions connected to broader company goals.

The article notes that not every company needs a full-time technology executive. Smaller businesses may instead need experienced guidance for certain projects or a limited number of hours. Warning signs can include rising technology costs, repeated cybersecurity concerns, unsuccessful projects, or leaders spending too much time managing technology questions.

A lack of shared planning may provide another warning sign. When departments make separate technology decisions, businesses can face higher costs, security gaps, and software problems. The article explains that a shared technology strategy can provide clearer direction across the organization.

Ultimately, the article explains that the value of a Fractional CIO centers on planning and leadership rather than daily troubleshooting. Strong technology guidance can help businesses organize decisions about systems, security, spending, growth, and long-term needs.

When a Business Needs a Fractional CIO features insights from Lionel Fermin, Managed IT Expert of Hobbs, New Mexico, in HelloNation.

#5459. Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, quickly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.)

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill said. “We went with commodity memory.”

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

“One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very quickly,” McCaskill said. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”

#5458. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/19 to correct that Charlie Trillingham worked for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business, not the Foster School itself.

#5457. Defense tech VC hit a record $37.9 billion last quarter. Two investors say it looks like 2021

When it comes to defense tech, it’s a FOMO-YOLO market, two prominent investors in the sector said onstage this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

“I’m a long-term optimist and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” said Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners.

“There are a lot of new entrants into the space. The death of SaaS and the disruption from AI has shifted capital into areas of deep tech, space, robotics, energy, and defense,” he said. “There’s folks deploying capital who aren’t experts in any one of those sectors. So, consequently, we can talk about a bubble.”

The money has arrived fast. Venture capitalists put a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 117.5% from the prior quarter, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune in its coverage of defense tech CEOs at the forum. Valuations have climbed with it: Early-stage defense startups have fetched 17 to 50 times revenue, Fortune reported this summer.

Even the sector’s biggest winners are uneasy. Anduril cofounder Trae Stephens told Fortune in June that mid-stage defense startups trade at multiples that are “completely disconnected from reality.”

Aidan Madigan-Curtis, a partner at venture firm Eclipse, described the mood bluntly.

“There is a pretty big YOLO sentiment happening right now, essentially in physical tech investing,” Madigan-Curtis said. “There are a lot of tourist investors who are excited about a person, a background, a theme… [and] maybe they’re most excited about who invested in the last round and the signal that that gives, versus a hardcore underwriting of a real set of capabilities that can truly pierce into a market.”

That froth now meets a broader shock. Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12, under pressure from the chipmaker’s board, has left the startup ecosystem primed for change and possible disruption.

AI startups are most exposed, but private capital markets more broadly are in flux, including the deep-tech bets now crowding into defense.

For startups, the harder test is selling to the government. It has long been a difficult market to crack, and the Pentagon, which has used the name Department of War as a secondary title since a 2025 executive order, is among the hardest. Part of the trouble is that government isn’t a monolithic customer, even if it looks like one.

“There’s a misconception that the Pentagon is this all-or-nothing type of customer,” said Faltas. “It’s actually not. The building itself is… called the Pentagon. It’s got five corners, and each of those five corners needs to be engaged with, and educated with, and listened to… That requires a very focused ground game.”

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5455. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5454. Microsoft’s CFO admits she joined the tech giant without even knowing her salary—and then missed her first day of work

As an economics undergraduate at Duke University in the 1990s, Amy Hood had no master plan that would one day land her the top finance job at one of the world’s biggest tech companies.

In fact, now Microsoft’s chief financial officer, Hood, said her career has looked more like a roller coaster than a ladder—and the lesson she told the class of 2026 still resonates today.

“As you start out, many successful careers are rarely—if ever—a straight line,” she said at Duke’s commencement ceremony in May. “Your next step doesn’t have to be a perfect one. It just has to be an opportunity.”

Hood learned that the hard way. After graduating from Duke in 1994, she built her early career at Goldman Sachs and later earned her MBA from Harvard. But over time, she realized corporate banking wasn’t how she wanted to spend the rest of her life. So she quit—without much of a plan of what would come next.

She considered going back to school for a third degree, but eventually stumbled upon what seemed like a perfect reset: an internship with the National Park Service.

“I thought, this is perfect. It’s a sign—I’ll get assigned to Yosemite or Yellowstone, someplace iconic,” Hood recalled. “I’ll work outdoors, I’ll live somewhere beautiful, and feel the space and energy that nature provides.”

Instead, the then-30-year-old was assigned to a less glamorous spot: Alcatraz Island, or as she called it, “a prison on a rock.” Not the manifestation she had imagined, she quit after a single day.

Months later, after an extended job search, a friend called and asked whether she wanted to interview at Microsoft—even though she had already faced two rejections from the company. This time, she landed a role in investor relations and accepted the offer without even asking about the salary.

“It was a job, a step forward, and truthfully, I needed a paycheck,” she said.

Even then, her start at Microsoft in 2002 was rocky. Hood admitted she missed her first day after miscalculating how long it would take to drive her silver Volvo from California to Seattle.

Still, the gamble paid off. Over the next decade, Hood steadily rose through the company’s ranks before being named CFO in 2013. Microsoft’s business has thrived under her leadership, and it ranks highly on Fortune’s lists of World’s Most Admired and America’s Most Innovative Companies. In 2025 alone, she earned $29.5 million in total compensation.

For today’s college graduates, Hood’s winding path to the top may feel increasingly out of reach as many young workers struggle to land even their first full-time job. Companies across the tech industry—including Microsoft—have cut thousands of roles in recent years as businesses restructure and ramp up investments in artificial intelligence.

The uncertainty has weighed heavily on young workers. More than 60% of the class of 2026 are pessimistic about their career prospects, according to a report from Handshake.

At the same time, many graduates are entering the workforce with expectations that are not aligned with today’s labor market. College seniors surveyed by real estate platform Clever said they expect to earn roughly $80,000 within a year of graduating. But the average starting salary for recent graduates is closer to $56,000—a gap of nearly $24,000.

Hood acknowledged the uncertainty facing Gen Z, but argued that many young workers are more prepared than they think. The bigger challenge, she said, is letting go of the expectation that they need to have everything figured out immediately.

“I can’t believe I’m saying this to some of the most accomplished young people on the planet, but maybe lower your bar a little,” she said. “Be open that something may not be exactly right, but could turn out to be a perfect place to learn about yourself—what you like, what you don’t. All the steps matter, and it took me decades to figure that out.”

She also urged graduates to stay adaptable and curious in a world that is changing faster than any previous generation has experienced.

“You will figure out who you are by stepping in and letting people push back, by doing things that scare you just a little, by raising your hand when you’re pretty sure you don’t have the right answer, and by taking a job that doesn’t make sense on paper but makes sense to you,” she told graduates.

And when setbacks inevitably happen, Hood said resilience matters more than perfection.

“Remember, there aren’t that many one-way doors—so go through a few of those things. And if you get a no, just try a new door,” she said. “Every step builds confidence, even the ones that feel like mistakes at the time—especially those. After all, the best stories always come from those moments.”

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on May 11, 2026.

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5452. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5451. Tech investor Bill Gurley says workers who went through the ‘college conveyor belt’ and chased safe jobs are at high risk of AI automation

Professionals have taught for generations that succeeding in school and attending an elite university would guarantee a rewarding six-figure career. But within a matter of years, AI has disrupted the world of work, and it’s quickly taking over the office roles humans were once promised.

Now, venture capitalist Bill Gurley cautions workers against blindly following the career blueprint.

“This is new and fast, and it’s attacking jobs that haven’t been attacked in the past,” Gurley said during the On with Kara Swisher podcast earlier this year. “It’s creating a lot of anxiety, but I don’t know that we can put it back in the bottle.”

The prolific tech financier, famous for his early investments in Uber and Zillow, is skeptical the government could pass AI regulation or pull off a massive reskilling effort. So as the technology continues to automate traditionally stable and lucrative roles, like lawyers and software engineers, it’s imperative workers actually be invested in their profession—or risk facing the chopping block.

“The people that are most at risk are the ones that are sitting idly in the job and don’t really have a why or a purpose for it,” Gurley said. “A lot of the people that go through that college conveyor belt, that are chasing a safe job, that end up working as a widget or a cog in an industry they may not love—I think they are ripe for disruption.”

The Benchmark Capital general partner acknowledges it’s easier said than done, but the best plan is to “craft your own career path” and tailor it to an individual’s distinct skills.

For those who can’t switch sectors or become self-employed, AI can act as career “jet fuel” that can make them even better at their jobs and indispensable to their employers.

“If it’s out of your control, I just would say understand what it’s capable of in your industry and be the most AI-aware person in your job,” Gurley advised. “You’re going to then be the last person that they want to get rid of.”

Gurley explores the idea that chasing a career of passion is a strategic edge, and not fluffy advice, in his newest book Runnin’ Down a Dream. He’s also one of several business leaders questioning the efficacy of how young professionals are trained to approach college.

The investor has noticed a few worrying trends that may inhibit young professionals from following their true aspirations, hurting their career success. Gurley explained that kids today are “programmed from a time perspective” more than other generations. The budding talent start worrying about having a stacked résumé from a young age, and now some colleges require students to apply with a major in mind.

These restraints don’t allow them to freely explore what jobs they’d enjoy, instead funneling them into a professional path very quickly. He believes that’s part of the reason why so many people are checked out at work—a group that’s most susceptible to disruption.

“There seems to me to be somewhat of a problem out there in that people aren’t landing where they’re passionate about what they’re doing,” Gurley said. “I don’t think it’s anyone’s fault, but I think we’ve turned the college matriculation process into this pressure cooker.”

Former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky echoes some of Gurley’s philosophy about career success in the AI era. Workers won’t be able to simply coast on a glitzy Ivy League degree: They need to have passion for their professions and the necessary tech skills to succeed in their careers.

“My guess is that the future of work belongs not anymore to the people that have the fanciest degrees or went to the best colleges,” Roslansky said during a fireside chat at the platform’s San Francisco office last year.

Instead, he predicted talent most likely to land a job and succeed are “the people who are adaptable, forward thinking, ready to learn, and ready to embrace these tools…It really kind of opens up the playing field in a way that I think we’ve never seen before.”

Fei-Fei Li, a Stanford professor and CEO of AI startup World Labs, dubbed the “Godmother of AI,” says being tech-savvy on the job matters more than anything else.

Now it’s essential for professionals to “superpower” themselves quickly with the tools, she advised.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 3, 2026.

Emma Burleigh is a reporter at Fortune, covering success, careers, entrepreneurship, and personal finance. Before joining the Success desk, she co-authored Fortune’s CHRO Daily newsletter, extensively covering the workplace and the future of jobs. Emma has also written for publications including the Observer and The China Project, publishing long-form stories on culture, entertainment, and geopolitics.
